about: LAWS0007 is UCL Laws' compulsory 30-credit first-year module on the criminal law of England and Wales, taught in person across Terms 1 and 2 and assessed in 2026/27 by a 100% examination. It begins with the structure of criminal liability, actus reus, mens rea and the courts' role, moves through basic concepts (omissions, causation, recklessness), then criminal damage, non-fatal offences and consent, homicide and intention, theft and fraud, and ends with denials of offences and rationale-based defences. This pack follows that order, splitting some syllabus areas into two topics.
topics: Introduction: the structure of criminal liability and the courts' role
Homicide: manslaughter and the partial defences
Denials of offences: automatism, insanity, mistake and intoxication
Rationale-based defences: self-defence, duress and necessity

notes.body:
Criminal liability in England and Wales is usually analysed by breaking an offence into its elements and then asking whether any defence applies. Learning to do this cleanly is the core skill for problem questions throughout the module.

Sources of criminal law
- Statute creates most offences (e.g. the Theft Act 1968, the Criminal Damage Act 1971, the Fraud Act 2006).
- Some major offences are still defined by the common law, notably murder and manslaughter, although statute has modified them (e.g. the Homicide Act 1957 and the Coroners and Justice Act 2009).
- The courts no longer create new offences. In R v Jones (Margaret) [2006] UKHL 16 the House of Lords said that creating crimes is now a matter for Parliament. The courts do still develop existing offences: in R v R [1992] 1 AC 599 the House of Lords held that the supposed marital exemption to rape was no longer part of the law.

Actus reus and mens rea
- Actus reus is the external element: the conduct, any surrounding circumstances and, for result crimes, the consequence (e.g. death in homicide).
- Mens rea is the fault element required for each part of the actus reus: intention, knowledge, belief, recklessness or, for some offences, negligence.
- A complete analysis also asks whether D has a defence.

The burden and standard of proof
Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462 established the "golden thread": the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Where D raises a defence such as self-defence, D bears only an evidential burden; the prosecution must then disprove it. Insanity and some statutory defences are exceptions, where D must prove the defence on the balance of probabilities.

Coincidence of actus reus and mens rea
The two elements must coincide in time, but the courts interpret this flexibly.
- Continuing acts: in Fagan v Metropolitan Police Commissioner [1969] 1 QB 439, D accidentally drove onto a police officer's foot and then deliberately left the car there. The battery was a continuing act and mens rea arose during it.
- Single transaction: in Thabo Meli v R [1954] 1 WLR 228 (PC), defendants who believed they had killed V and then threw the "body" over a cliff, where V died of exposure, were guilty of murder because the whole series of acts was one transaction.

Strict liability
Some offences, mostly regulatory, require no mens rea as to at least one element. There is a strong presumption that Parliament intends mens rea to be required (Sweet v Parsley [1970] AC 132; B v DPP [2000] 2 AC 428). The presumption can be displaced by clear words or necessary implication, which is more likely where the offence is regulatory, concerns public safety and strict liability would promote compliance (Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v A-G of Hong Kong [1985] AC 1).

Legality
Article 7 ECHR prohibits retrospective criminal liability, and English law requires offences to be stated with reasonable certainty. In CR v UK and SW v UK (1995) the European Court of Human Rights held that convictions based on the removal of the marital exemption did not breach Article 7, because the development was reasonably foreseeable. (CR v UK was R's own application; SW was convicted in a separate case.)

Exam tips: For every offence, list the actus reus and mens rea elements, deal with each in turn using authority, and only then turn to defences. Say who bears which burden.

Omissions
English law does not impose a general duty to act. A person is liable for failing to act only if (1) the offence can be committed by omission (murder and manslaughter can; many statutory offences are framed in terms of acts) and (2) D was under a duty to act and failed to do what was reasonable.

Recognised duty situations:
- Statute, e.g. the offence of wilful neglect of a child under the Children and Young Persons Act 1933.
- Contract: in R v Pittwood (1902), a railway gatekeeper who left a level crossing gate open was guilty of manslaughter when a cart was hit by a train.
- Special relationship: parents owe duties to children (R v Gibbins and Proctor (1918), a child starved to death).
- Voluntary assumption of care: in R v Stone and Dobinson [1977] QB 354, D and his partner took in his anorexic sister and then failed to get help as she deteriorated.
- Creating a dangerous situation: in R v Miller [1983] 2 AC 161, a squatter fell asleep with a lit cigarette, woke to find the mattress smouldering and simply moved rooms. Once aware of the danger he had created, he was under a duty to take reasonable steps to counteract it. In R v Evans [2009] EWCA Crim 650, D supplied heroin to her half-sister, who self-injected; D realised her sister had overdosed but did not seek help. A duty arose because D had contributed to a life-threatening situation.
- Public office: a police officer who watched a man being beaten to death was guilty of misconduct in public office (R v Dytham [1979] QB 722).

Withdrawing life-sustaining treatment is treated as an omission. In Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789, doctors could lawfully stop treating a patient in a persistent vegetative state because continuing was no longer in his best interests, so there was no duty to continue.

Causation
For result crimes the prosecution must prove factual and legal causation.

Factual causation uses the "but for" test. In R v White [1910] 2 KB 124, D poisoned his mother's drink but she died of an unrelated heart attack: he was guilty of attempted murder only.

Legal causation requires that D's conduct was an operating and more than minimal cause of the result. It need not be the only cause.
- Medical treatment rarely breaks the chain. In R v Smith [1959] 2 QB 35, the original stab wound was still an operating and substantial cause despite poor treatment. In R v Cheshire [1991] 1 WLR 844, negligent treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent of D's acts and so potent in causing death that D's contribution becomes insignificant. R v Jordan (1956), where the wound had largely healed and treatment was "palpably wrong", is an exceptional case.
- Switching off life support after brain-stem death does not break the chain (R v Malcherek and Steel [1981] 1 WLR 690).
- Third-party acts: a free, deliberate and informed act of an adult breaks the chain. In R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] UKHL 38, D who prepared a syringe of heroin for V was not guilty of manslaughter when V self-injected and died. A reasonable act of self-preservation is not free: in R v Pagett (1983) 76 Cr App R 279, D used his pregnant girlfriend as a shield and fired at police, who shot back and killed her.
- Victim's escape: injuries suffered while fleeing are caused by D unless the victim's response was so "daft" or out of proportion that it was a new act (R v Roberts (1971); R v Williams and Davis [1992] 1 WLR 380).
- The thin skull rule: D takes the victim as he finds him, including the victim's beliefs. In R v Blaue [1975] 1 WLR 1411, a Jehovah's Witness who refused a blood transfusion after being stabbed died; D was still the cause.

Exam tips: For omissions, name the duty category and say what reasonable step D failed to take. For causation, deal with factual causation first, then test each possible intervening act against the specific case law.

Mens rea terms are not used in the same way across every offence, so you need to know the standard meanings and the leading cases.

Intention
Intention is the most serious fault element. It is examined in detail under homicide (direct intention and the Woollin test for oblique intention).

Recklessness: from Cunningham to R v G
- R v Cunningham [1957] 2 QB 396: D tore a gas meter from a wall to steal money; gas seeped into the next-door house. "Maliciously" in s23 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 required that D foresaw the risk of harm and went on to take it. This is subjective recklessness.
- MPC v Caldwell [1982] AC 341 introduced an objective test for criminal damage: D was reckless if he created an obvious risk and either gave no thought to it or recognised it and went on anyway. In Elliott v C (1983), magistrates acquitted a 14-year-old girl with learning difficulties of arson because she had not appreciated the risk, but the Divisional Court held that Caldwell required her to be treated as reckless, although the risk would not have been obvious to her.
- R v G [2003] UKHL 50 overruled Caldwell. Two boys aged 11 and 12 set fire to newspapers behind a shop, expecting the fire to burn out; it spread and caused about £1 million of damage. The House of Lords held that a person acts recklessly as to a circumstance when aware of a risk that it exists or will exist, and as to a result when aware of a risk that it will occur, and it is, in the circumstances known to him, unreasonable to take the risk. This follows clause 18(c) of the Law Commission's draft Criminal Code.

Reasons given in R v G:
- Conviction for a serious crime should depend on proof of a culpable state of mind.
- Caldwell had misinterpreted Parliament's intention in the Criminal Damage Act 1971, which was meant to keep the subjective meaning of "maliciously".
- Caldwell could produce obvious unfairness, especially to children and people of limited capacity.
- The decision had been widely criticised.

The R v G test is now the general meaning of recklessness in criminal law. For example, the Court of Appeal applied it to misconduct in public office in Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 2003) [2004] EWCA Crim 868.

Knowledge and belief
Some offences require D to know or believe a circumstance, e.g. handling stolen goods "knowing or believing them to be stolen" (Theft Act 1968, s22). Knowledge is a higher standard than recklessness.

Negligence
Negligence is objective: falling below the standard of the reasonable person. It is rare as the fault element for serious crimes, but it underlies gross negligence manslaughter and many driving offences.

Transferred malice
If D has the mens rea for an offence against one victim and causes the actus reus of the same offence against another, the mens rea transfers.
- R v Latimer (1886): D swung a belt at one man, missed and hit a woman; guilty of malicious wounding.
- R v Pembliton (1874): D threw a stone at people and broke a window. Malice does not transfer between different kinds of offence, so he was not guilty of criminal damage unless reckless as to the property.
- Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 1994) [1998] AC 245: D stabbed a pregnant woman; the child was born prematurely and died. The House of Lords refused a "double transfer" of malice to support murder, but D could be guilty of unlawful act manslaughter.

Exam tips: In problem answers, state the R v G test fully and apply both limbs: was D aware of the risk, and was it unreasonable to take it? Do not use Caldwell except as history.

The Criminal Damage Act 1971 (CDA) creates a basic offence, an aggravated offence and arson.

Basic offence: s1(1)
A person commits the offence if, without lawful excuse, he destroys or damages any property belonging to another, intending to do so or being reckless as to whether it would be destroyed or damaged. It is triable either way, with a maximum of 10 years on indictment (s4).

Actus reus
- Property (s10(1)) means property of a tangible nature, real or personal, including money and some animals; wild mushrooms, flowers, fruit and foliage are excluded.
- Belonging to another (s10(2)): anyone with custody or control, or a proprietary right or interest, counts as an owner.
- Damage is a question of fact and degree. It includes impairment of value or usefulness, and temporary harm that costs time or money to remove. In Hardman v Chief Constable of Avon and Somerset [1986] Crim LR 330, painting silhouettes in water-soluble paint was damage because the council paid to clean it off. By contrast, spitting on a police officer's raincoat, which could be wiped off, was not damage (A (a juvenile) v R [1978] Crim LR 689).

Mens rea
D must intend or be reckless (R v G [2003] UKHL 50) both as to damaging property and as to the fact that it belongs to another. In R v Smith (David) [1974] QB 354, a tenant who damaged fixtures he had installed, honestly believing they were his own, lacked mens rea even though his belief was legally wrong and probably unreasonable.

Lawful excuse: s5
Section 5 applies to the s1(1) offence, not the aggravated offence.
- s5(2)(a): D believed that the person entitled to consent had consented, or would have consented if they had known the circumstances.
- s5(2)(b): D acted to protect property which he believed was in immediate need of protection, and believed the means used were reasonable in all the circumstances.
- s5(3): it does not matter whether the belief was justified, if it was honestly held.

Cases on s5:
- Jaggard v Dickinson [1981] QB 527: D, drunk, broke into a house she believed was her friend's. Her honest belief that the friend would consent gave her a defence even though it was caused by intoxication.
- Blake v DPP [1993] Crim LR 586: a vicar who wrote on a pillar near Parliament, claiming God's consent, had no s5(2)(a) defence.
- R v Hill and Hall (1989) 89 Cr App R 74: whether D acted "in order to protect property" is decided objectively; the risk feared was too remote.

Aggravated criminal damage: s1(2)
D destroys or damages any property (including his own), intending to destroy or damage it or being reckless as to that, and intending to endanger life by the destruction or damage or being reckless as to whether life would be endangered. No life need actually be endangered. The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.
- R v Steer [1988] AC 111: D fired a rifle at the windows of a house. The danger to life must come from the damage itself, not from the act causing it (the bullets).
- R v Webster; R v Warwick [1995] 2 All ER 168: where D throws a heavy object onto a vehicle and the damage (e.g. a shattered windscreen or falling debris) could endanger life, s1(2) can be satisfied.

Arson: s1(3)
Damage by fire is charged as arson, with a maximum of life imprisonment.

Exam tips: Check whose property it is and whether D believed it was his own (Smith), and whether a s5 belief arises. For s1(2), identify the damage and ask whether D intended or foresaw that this damage would endanger life.

The non-fatal offences form a ladder of seriousness. Most come from the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 (OAPA), which is often criticised as outdated; the Law Commission recommended replacing it in its 2015 report (Law Com No 361), but this has not been done.

Common assault and battery
Both are summary offences charged under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988.
- Assault: causing V to apprehend immediate unlawful force. Words, and even silence, can be enough: in R v Ireland [1998] AC 147, silent phone calls could be an assault if V feared violence might come within a short time. Words can also negate an assault (Tuberville v Savage (1669)).
- Battery: the application of unlawful force, however slight. Ordinary physical contact of everyday life is impliedly accepted (Collins v Wilcock [1984] 1 WLR 1172). Force can be applied indirectly: in Haystead v Chief Constable of Derbyshire [2000] 3 All ER 890, D punched a woman who dropped her baby, which was a battery on the baby.
- Mens rea: intention or recklessness as to causing apprehension or applying force (R v Venna [1976] QB 421; R v Savage [1992] 1 AC 699).

Assault occasioning actual bodily harm: s47 OAPA
- Actus reus: an assault or battery that causes ABH. ABH is any hurt or injury calculated to interfere with health or comfort (R v Miller [1954] 2 QB 282), and it must be more than transient or trifling (R v Donovan [1934] 2 KB 498). It includes a recognised psychiatric condition but not mere fear or panic (R v Chan-Fook [1994] 1 WLR 689), and can include cutting off hair (DPP v Smith [2006] EWHC 94 (Admin)).
- Mens rea: only that for the assault or battery. D need not foresee any harm (R v Roberts (1971), where V jumped from D's moving car; R v Savage).
- Maximum: 5 years.

Unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting GBH: s20 OAPA
- Wound: a break in both layers of the skin (JCC v Eisenhower [1984] QB 331, where internal bleeding in the eye was not a wound).
- GBH means "really serious harm" (DPP v Smith [1961] AC 290), judged in light of V's age and health (R v Bollom [2003] EWCA Crim 2846).
- "Inflict" does not require an assault. In R v Burstow [1998] AC 147, stalking that caused severe depression was inflicting GBH.
- Mens rea: "maliciously" means intention or recklessness as to causing some harm, not necessarily serious harm (R v Mowatt [1968] 1 QB 421; DPP v Parmenter [1992] 1 AC 699).
- Maximum: 5 years.

Wounding or causing GBH with intent: s18 OAPA
- Actus reus: wounding or causing GBH ("cause" is wider than "inflict").
- Mens rea: intention to cause GBH, or, where D wounds or causes GBH, intention to resist or prevent lawful arrest. Intention has the Woollin meaning.
- Maximum: life imprisonment.

Common exam trap
In R v Savage, D threw beer over V intending only to soak her; the glass slipped and cut V. There was no finding that she foresaw any physical harm, so the Court of Appeal quashed her s20 conviction and substituted s47; the House of Lords upheld the s47 conviction because she intended the battery and ABH resulted.

Racially or religiously aggravated forms of these offences exist under the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 (s29).

Exam tips: Identify the harm first (no injury, ABH, wound or GBH), then pick the offence and check its specific mens rea. Explain the "constructive" nature of s47 and s20, where the mens rea does not match the harm.

Consent is central to the non-fatal offences. Whether it is classed as a defence or as negating the "unlawfulness" of force, the practical questions are: can V consent to this level of harm, and was V's consent real?

The general rule
- V can consent to an assault or battery.
- V cannot consent to ABH or more serious harm unless the activity falls within a recognised exception. In Attorney-General's Reference (No 6 of 1980) [1981] QB 715, two youths agreed to settle a quarrel with a fist fight in the street; consent was no defence because it is not in the public interest that people should cause each other ABH for no good reason.
- R v Brown [1994] 1 AC 212: consenting adults who engaged in sadomasochistic activity causing wounds and ABH were guilty under s47 and s20. The majority (3-2) refused to create a new exception, emphasising public policy and the risk of more serious harm and infection. The dissenting judges stressed personal autonomy and privacy.

Recognised exceptions
- Properly conducted sports. In R v Barnes [2004] EWCA Crim 3246, the Court of Appeal held that injuries in contact sports should be prosecuted only where the conduct is sufficiently grave to be criminal; relevant factors include the type of sport, the level, the nature of the act, the degree of force and D's state of mind.
- Surgery, tattooing and piercing.
- Rough horseplay, including genuine belief in consent (R v Jones (1986); R v Aitken [1992] 1 WLR 1006).
- Personal adornment: in R v Wilson [1997] QB 47, a husband who branded his initials on his wife's buttocks at her request was not guilty; the court compared it to tattooing.
- Consensual risk of sexually transmitted infection: V can consent to the risk of infection if the consent is informed (R v Dica [2004] EWCA Crim 1103; R v Konzani [2005] EWCA Crim 706). Consent to sex is not consent to the risk of infection where D has concealed it.

Limits
- R v Emmett (1999): consent was no defence where D's sexual activity caused his partner burns and a risk of asphyxiation.
- R v BM [2018] EWCA Crim 560: a "body modifier" who removed a customer's ear and nipple and split a tongue could not rely on consent; the court refused to extend the tattooing exception to these procedures.
- Domestic Abuse Act 2021, s71: for offences under ss18, 20 and 47 OAPA, it is not a defence that V consented to the infliction of serious harm for the purposes of sexual gratification. There is an exception for some s20 and s47 cases involving sexually transmitted infection where V consented to the risk. The section states the existing law in Brown and Emmett.

Is the consent real?
- Capacity: children may lack capacity to consent, e.g. to tattooing (Burrell v Harmer [1967] Crim LR 169).
- Fraud: consent is vitiated if V is deceived as to D's identity or the nature or quality of the act. In R v Tabassum [2000] 2 Cr App R 328, women consented to breast examinations for medical purposes, not to touching for other purposes, so there was no true consent. In R v Richardson [1999] QB 444, a dentist who had been suspended was not guilty: patients were not deceived about her identity or the nature of the treatment.
- Sexual offences have their own statutory rules on consent (Sexual Offences Act 2003, ss74-76), which are outside this topic.

Exam tips: First identify the level of harm. If it is only assault or battery, consent will usually work. If it is ABH or more, ask whether a recognised exception applies, whether V's consent was informed and real, and whether s71 applies. Be ready to evaluate Brown from both the paternalist and autonomy perspectives.

Murder is a common law offence: the unlawful killing of a human being under the King's peace with malice aforethought. It carries a mandatory life sentence.

Actus reus
- D must cause the death of a person "in being". A foetus is not a person in being until born alive with an existence independent of its mother (Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 1994) [1998] AC 245).
- The old "year and a day" rule was abolished by the Law Reform (Year and a Day Rule) Act 1996; the Attorney General's consent is needed for a prosecution in some cases where death occurs more than three years after the injury.
- Causation follows the general rules (see acts, omissions and causation).

Mens rea: malice aforethought
Malice aforethought means an intention to kill or an intention to cause grievous bodily harm (R v Vickers [1957] 2 QB 664; R v Cunningham [1982] AC 566). The GBH rule is controversial because D can be a murderer without intending or foreseeing death.

Direct intention
D intends a result if it is his aim or purpose: the result D acts in order to bring about (R v Mohan [1976] QB 1). Motive is irrelevant.

Oblique (indirect) intention
The courts have struggled with cases where death is not D's aim but a side effect of achieving it.
- R v Moloney [1985] AC 905: foresight of consequences is evidence of intention, not intention itself. Lord Bridge's "natural consequence" guidelines proved misleading.
- R v Hancock and Shankland [1986] AC 455: striking miners dropped a concrete block onto a taxi. The greater the probability of the consequence, the more likely it was foreseen and intended, but the Moloney guidelines needed explaining to juries.
- R v Nedrick [1986] 1 WLR 1025: the jury was not entitled to infer intention unless death or serious harm was a virtual certainty and D appreciated this.
- R v Woollin [1999] 1 AC 82: D threw his three-month-old son onto a hard surface. The House of Lords approved Nedrick with one change: the jury is not entitled to find the necessary intention unless death or serious bodily harm was a virtual certainty (barring some unforeseen intervention) as a result of D's actions and D appreciated that this was the case. The murder conviction was quashed and manslaughter substituted.
- R v Matthews and Alleyne [2003] EWCA Crim 192: Woollin is a rule of evidence. Foresight of virtual certainty does not automatically equal intention; the jury may, but need not, find intention.

The Woollin test was applied outside murder in Re A (Children) (Conjoined Twins) [2001] Fam 147, where separating twins would inevitably kill the weaker twin; the surgeons would have the necessary intention, but their act was lawful through necessity.

Foresight and complicity
In R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8 the Supreme Court corrected the law of secondary liability: an accessory must intend to assist or encourage the crime, and foresight that the principal might commit it is only evidence of that intention. This mirrors the Woollin distinction between foresight and intention.

Reform
The Law Commission's 2006 report (Law Com No 304) proposed dividing murder into degrees and codifying intention, but only its proposals on partial defences were enacted (Coroners and Justice Act 2009).

Exam tips: Start with direct intention. Only if death or GBH was not D's purpose, give the Woollin direction in full and explain that the jury "may find" intention. Remember intention to cause GBH is enough for murder.

Manslaughter is voluntary (murder plus a partial defence) or involuntary (no mens rea for murder). The sentence is discretionary, up to life.

Voluntary manslaughter: loss of control
The Coroners and Justice Act 2009 (CJA 2009), ss54-56, replaced provocation (abolished by s56) from 4 October 2010. Under s54(1) D is not guilty of murder if:
- (a) D's acts or omissions in killing resulted from a loss of self-control, which need not be sudden (s54(2));
- (b) the loss of self-control had a qualifying trigger; and
- (c) a person of D's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in D's circumstances, might have reacted in the same or a similar way.
The defence is not available if D acted in a considered desire for revenge (s54(4)).

Qualifying triggers (s55):
- fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person; and/or
- things done or said that constituted circumstances of an extremely grave character and caused D to have a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged.
A trigger is disregarded if D incited it to provide an excuse for violence (s55(6)(a)-(b); R v Dawes [2013] EWCA Crim 322). Sexual infidelity must be disregarded as a thing done or said (s55(6)(c)), but in R v Clinton [2012] EWCA Crim 2 the Court of Appeal held it can be considered as context when another trigger is relied on.

D's circumstances in (c) exclude matters whose only relevance is to D's general capacity for tolerance or self-restraint (s54(3)), and voluntary intoxication is not relevant (R v Asmelash [2013] EWCA Crim 157). D bears only an evidential burden; if sufficient evidence is adduced, the prosecution must disprove the defence (s54(5)-(6)).

Voluntary manslaughter: diminished responsibility
Section 2 Homicide Act 1957, as substituted by s52 CJA 2009, requires an abnormality of mental functioning which:
- (a) arose from a recognised medical condition;
- (b) substantially impaired D's ability to understand the nature of his conduct, form a rational judgment, or exercise self-control; and
- (c) provides an explanation for the killing, i.e. it caused or was a significant contributory factor in causing D's conduct.
D must prove it on the balance of probabilities. In R v Golds [2016] UKSC 61 the Supreme Court held that "substantially" means important or weighty, not merely more than trivial. Voluntary acute intoxication is not a recognised medical condition for this purpose (R v Dowds [2012] EWCA Crim 281).

Involuntary manslaughter: unlawful act (constructive) manslaughter
- An unlawful act that is a crime, not merely a civil wrong, and normally an act rather than an omission. In R v Lamb [1967] 2 QB 981 there was no assault, so no unlawful act.
- The act must be dangerous: one which all sober and reasonable people would inevitably recognise must subject V to at least the risk of some harm (R v Church [1966] 1 QB 59). D need not realise this (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977] AC 500).
- The reasonable person has D's knowledge. In R v Dawson (1985) 81 Cr App R 150, robbers did not know of their victim's heart condition. In R v Watson [1989] 1 WLR 684, the frail elderly victim's condition would have been obvious to a burglar during the burglary.
- The harm foreseen need not be the type that caused death (R v JM and SM [2012] EWCA Crim 2293).

Involuntary manslaughter: gross negligence
R v Adomako [1995] 1 AC 171: an anaesthetist failed to notice a disconnected tube. The elements are:
- a duty of care owed by D to V;
- breach of that duty;
- a serious and obvious risk of death that was reasonably foreseeable at the time of breach, based on what D knew (R v Rose [2017] EWCA Crim 1168, an optometrist);
- the breach caused death, proved to the criminal standard (R v Broughton [2020] EWCA Crim 1093); and
- the negligence was so bad that, in the jury's view, it should be judged criminal.

Exam tips: If D had the mens rea for murder, consider the partial defences. If not, consider unlawful act and gross negligence manslaughter separately, naming the criminal offence that is the unlawful act.

Theft is defined in s1(1) of the Theft Act 1968: a person is guilty if he dishonestly appropriates property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it. The maximum sentence is 7 years (s7). Sections 2-6 explain each element.

Appropriation: s3
- Any assumption by a person of the rights of an owner, including a later assumption by keeping or dealing with property as owner (s3(1)).
- Assuming any one of the owner's rights is enough (R v Morris [1984] AC 320, swapping price labels in a supermarket).
- Appropriation can occur even where the owner consents (Lawrence v MPC [1972] AC 626; DPP v Gomez [1993] AC 442, where a shop manager was tricked into authorising a sale against dud cheques).
- Receiving a gift that is valid in civil law can be appropriation (R v Hinks [2001] 2 AC 241). The safeguard against over-criminalisation is the dishonesty requirement.
- A bona fide purchaser for value who later learns of a defect in title does not commit theft by keeping the property (s3(2)).

Property: s4
- Money and all other property, real or personal, including things in action and other intangible property (s4(1)).
- Land generally cannot be stolen except in limited cases (s4(2)).
- Wild mushrooms, flowers, fruit and foliage are not stolen if picked, unless for reward, sale or other commercial purpose (s4(3)).
- Confidential information is not property (Oxford v Moss (1979) 68 Cr App R 183, exam paper).

Belonging to another: s5
- Anyone having possession or control, or a proprietary right or interest (s5(1)). An owner can steal his own property from someone in possession (R v Turner (No 2) [1971] 1 WLR 901, car taken from a garage after repair).
- s5(3): property received under an obligation to retain and deal with it in a particular way. A travel agent was not guilty where there was no such obligation for deposits (R v Hall [1973] QB 126).
- s5(4): property got by another's mistake, where there is a legal obligation to restore it (Attorney-General's Reference (No 1 of 1983) [1985] QB 182, overpaid wages).

Intention of permanently depriving: s6
- Treating the property as one's own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights (s6(1)). Taking a car and demanding payment for its return falls within this (R v Raphael [2008] EWCA Crim 1014).
- Borrowing counts only if for a period and in circumstances equivalent to an outright taking. In R v Lloyd [1985] QB 829, films copied and returned undamaged were not stolen because their "goodness, virtue and practical value" had not gone.
- Taking money intending to replace it with equivalent notes is still an intention permanently to deprive of the specific notes (R v Velumyl [1989] Crim LR 299).

Dishonesty: s2 and the common law
Section 2(1) gives three cases where D is not dishonest: belief in a legal right to deprive, belief the owner would consent if he knew the circumstances, and belief the owner cannot be discovered by taking reasonable steps. Willingness to pay does not prevent dishonesty (s2(2)).

Otherwise dishonesty is decided by the test in Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67, which R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575 confirmed applies in criminal cases:
- first, establish D's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts (the genuineness of a belief is the question; its reasonableness is evidence of whether it was held);
- second, decide whether D's conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people.
There is no longer any requirement that D realised ordinary people would regard the conduct as dishonest, which was the second limb of R v Ghosh [1982] QB 1053. Ivey's discussion was strictly obiter, but in Barton and Booth a five-judge Court of Appeal held it must be followed.

Exam tips: Work through s3, s4, s5, s6 and dishonesty in order. Use s2(1) first, then Ivey. Remember that consent of the owner does not stop appropriation after Gomez and Hinks.

The Fraud Act 2006 came into force on 15 January 2007. It replaced the old deception offences in the Theft Acts 1968 and 1978 with a single offence of fraud, committed in one of three ways (s1). The maximum sentence on indictment is 10 years.

The old deception offences required that someone was actually deceived and that property or a service was obtained as a result. That caused problems where a machine was "deceived" or where it was unclear whether anyone was misled. Fraud under the 2006 Act is a conduct offence: no one need be deceived and no gain or loss need actually occur. What matters is D's conduct, dishonesty and ulterior intention.

Fraud by false representation: s2
D dishonestly makes a false representation, intending, by making it, to make a gain for himself or another, or to cause loss to another or expose another to a risk of loss.
- A representation is false if it is untrue or misleading and D knows that it is, or might be, untrue or misleading (s2(2)).
- It can be a representation as to fact or law, including a representation as to the state of mind of D or anyone else (s2(3)), e.g. a false promise to pay.
- It may be express or implied (s2(4)). Cases under the old law show implied representations by conduct: ordering a meal implies an intention to pay (DPP v Ray [1974] AC 370), and using a card implies authority to use it (R v Lambie [1982] AC 449).
- A representation is treated as made if submitted in any form to a system or device designed to receive, convey or respond to communications, with or without human intervention (s2(5)). Entering stolen card details at a self-checkout or online is covered.

Fraud by failing to disclose information: s3
D dishonestly fails to disclose information that he is under a legal duty to disclose, with the same intention as to gain or loss. Legal duties can arise from statute, from the terms of a contract, from custom, or from a fiduciary relationship.

Fraud by abuse of position: s4
D occupies a position in which he is expected to safeguard, or not to act against, the financial interests of another person, and dishonestly abuses that position, intending gain or loss. The abuse can be by omission (s4(2)). Typical positions are trustee and beneficiary, director and company, and employee and employer. In R v Valujevs [2014] EWCA Crim 2888, the Court of Appeal held that unlicensed gangmasters who controlled workers' pay and housing could occupy such a position; whether a position exists is partly a matter for the jury.

Gain and loss: s5
"Gain" and "loss" extend only to money or other property, whether temporary or permanent. Gain includes keeping what one has, and loss includes not getting what one might get.

Dishonesty
Dishonesty is judged by the Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67 test, which applies in criminal cases (R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575; Barton was convicted of fraud and other offences). Section 2 of the Theft Act 1968 does not apply to fraud.

Related offences
- Possessing or making articles for use in fraud (ss6-7).
- Obtaining services dishonestly (s11): unlike fraud, this is a result crime. D must actually obtain services, knowing that payment is or might be required, and intend to avoid paying. It covers, for example, climbing into a concert without a ticket.
- Common law conspiracy to defraud survives.

Exam tips: Choose the right form of fraud and set out each element in the statutory wording. Remember that s2 requires no one to be deceived and no money to change hands; the offence is complete when the representation is made.

notes.h: Denials of offences: automatism, insanity, mistake and intoxication
notes.body:
Some "defences" are really denials that the offence was committed: D says an element of the actus reus (usually voluntariness) or mens rea is missing. These include automatism, mistake and intoxication. Insanity is related, because it often arises when D pleads automatism, but it has its own rules.

Automatism
- An involuntary act: "an act which is done by the muscles without any control by the mind" (Lord Denning in Bratty v A-G for Northern Ireland [1963] AC 386).
- There must be a total destruction of voluntary control; reduced or impaired awareness is not enough (Attorney-General's Reference (No 2 of 1992) [1994] QB 91, a lorry driver "driving without awareness").
- Non-insane automatism requires an external cause, such as a blow to the head or an injection of insulin. In R v Quick [1973] QB 910, hypoglycaemia caused by insulin was external.
- If successful, D is acquitted.
- Self-induced automatism: for basic intent crimes, D cannot rely on automatism if he was reckless in bringing it about, e.g. knowing that failing to eat after insulin could make him aggressive or unpredictable (R v Bailey [1983] 1 WLR 760). Automatism caused by voluntary intoxication is governed by the intoxication rules.

Insanity
The M'Naghten Rules (1843) require D to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that he was labouring under such a defect of reason, from disease of the mind, as not to know the nature and quality of his act or, if he did know it, that he did not know it was wrong.
- "Disease of the mind" is a legal concept. Any internal cause affecting the mind counts: arteriosclerosis (R v Kemp [1957] 1 QB 399), epilepsy (R v Sullivan [1984] AC 156), hyperglycaemia from failing to take insulin (R v Hennessy [1989] 1 WLR 287) and sleepwalking (R v Burgess [1991] 2 QB 92).
- "Wrong" means both legally wrong and wrong by the standards of ordinary reasonable people (R v Keal [2022] EWCA Crim 341; see also R v Windle [1952] 2 QB 826). A defendant who knew the act was against the law cannot use this limb.
- The verdict is not guilty by reason of insanity. Under the Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964 (as amended), the court may make a hospital order, a supervision order or an absolute discharge.
- The internal/external distinction is criticised as arbitrary (compare Quick and Hennessy) and for labelling people with diabetes or epilepsy "insane".

Mistake
- A genuine mistake that means D lacks the mens rea required is a denial of the offence, whether or not it is reasonable (DPP v Morgan [1976] AC 182; B v DPP [2000] 2 AC 428). For rape and other sexual offences, statute now requires a reasonable belief in consent (Sexual Offences Act 2003, s1).
- In self-defence, D is judged on the facts as he genuinely believed them (R v Williams (Gladstone) [1987] 3 All ER 411).

Intoxication
- DPP v Majewski [1977] AC 443: voluntary intoxication can be relied on to show D lacked the mens rea for a specific intent offence (e.g. murder, s18, theft) but not for a basic intent offence (e.g. manslaughter, s20, s47, criminal damage under s1(1)). For basic intent crimes, getting voluntarily intoxicated is treated as sufficient fault (R v Lipman [1970] 1 QB 152). In R v Heard [2007] EWCA Crim 125, sexual assault was treated as a basic intent offence.
- Involuntary intoxication can negate mens rea, but if D still formed the intent there is no defence: "a drugged intent is still an intent" (R v Kingston [1995] 2 AC 355).
- Taking a non-dangerous drug, such as a sedative, may not be reckless, so the Majewski rule may not apply (R v Hardie [1985] 1 WLR 64).
- Dutch courage is no defence (A-G for Northern Ireland v Gallagher [1963] AC 349).
- A drunken mistake about the need for self-defence cannot be relied on (R v O'Grady [1987] QB 995; R v Hatton [2005] EWCA Crim 2951; s76(5) Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008).

Exam tips: Identify the cause of the condition first: internal points to insanity, external to automatism, alcohol or drugs to intoxication. Then classify the offence as specific or basic intent.

notes.h: Rationale-based defences: self-defence, duress and necessity
notes.body:
Unlike denials, these defences accept that D committed the offence (actus reus and mens rea) but offer a reason why D should not be convicted. Theorists often classify them as justifications (the conduct was permissible, even right, such as reasonable self-defence) or excuses (the conduct was wrong but D is not blameworthy, such as duress). This distinction helps explain the rules on who may resist, and why some defences are unavailable for murder.

Self-defence and prevention of crime
Self-defence at common law and the prevention of crime under s3 Criminal Law Act 1967 are clarified by s76 Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008. Two questions:
- Did D genuinely believe force was necessary? This is subjective: D is judged on the facts as he believed them, even if mistaken and unreasonable (R v Williams (Gladstone) [1987]; s76(3)-(4)). But a mistaken belief caused by voluntary intoxication cannot be relied on (s76(5)).
- Was the force used reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be? This is objective. Force is not reasonable if it was disproportionate (s76(6)).
- D cannot be expected to weigh the exact measure of force in the heat of the moment, and acting honestly and instinctively is strong evidence that the force was reasonable (s76(7)).
- There is no duty to retreat, but the possibility of retreat is a factor (s76(6A)). D need not wait to be struck first (Beckford v R [1988] AC 130).

Householder cases: s76(5A) provides that force that is grossly disproportionate is never reasonable. In R (Collins) v Secretary of State for Justice [2016] EWHC 33 (Admin), the Divisional Court held this means disproportionate (but not grossly disproportionate) force may be reasonable, not that it must be; the jury still decides. The Court of Appeal applied this two-stage approach in R v Ray [2017] EWCA Crim 1391.

Self-defence is a complete defence. There is no partial defence of excessive force; in a murder case, D might instead rely on loss of control (fear of serious violence).

Duress by threats
The leading authority is R v Hasan [2005] UKHL 22, building on R v Graham [1982] 1 WLR 294 (approved in R v Howe [1987] AC 417):
- a threat of death or serious injury;
- against D, his family or a person for whom he reasonably regards himself as responsible;
- D reasonably believed the threat was genuine and would be carried out immediately or almost immediately;
- a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing D's relevant characteristics would have responded in the same way (R v Bowen [1997] 1 WLR 372 on characteristics such as age, pregnancy, serious physical disability or recognised psychiatric condition);
- there was no evasive action D could reasonably have taken;
- D did not voluntarily associate with criminals when he ought reasonably to have foreseen the risk of being subjected to compulsion by threats of violence.
Duress is no defence to murder (Howe) or attempted murder (R v Gotts [1992] 2 AC 412).

Duress of circumstances
The same structure applies where the threat comes from circumstances rather than a person's demand (R v Willer (1986); R v Conway [1989] QB 290; R v Martin [1989] 1 All ER 652).

Necessity
- R v Dudley and Stephens (1884) 14 QBD 273: shipwrecked sailors who killed and ate the cabin boy were guilty of murder; necessity was no defence.
- Re A (Children) (Conjoined Twins) [2001] Fam 147: separating conjoined twins, which would inevitably kill the weaker twin to save the stronger, was lawful. Brooke LJ set out conditions: the act was needed to avoid inevitable and irreparable evil; no more was done than reasonably necessary; and the evil inflicted was not disproportionate to the evil avoided. The decision was limited to its unique facts.

Exam tips: For self-defence, separate the subjective belief question from the objective reasonableness question, and check whether it is a householder case. For duress, go through each Hasan requirement in order and remember the murder bar.

cards.b: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt (the 'golden thread'). Exceptions: insanity and certain statutory defences, where D bears a legal burden on the balance of probabilities.
Conduct (an act, or an omission where there is a duty), circumstances required by the offence definition, and, for result crimes, the consequence (e.g. death).
D accidentally drove onto an officer's foot and then refused to move. Battery was a continuing act, so mens rea formed during it coincided with the actus reus.
Privy Council: where D causes death through a series of acts forming one transaction, it is enough that mens rea existed during the transaction, even if death came from a later act.
House of Lords: there is a presumption that Parliament intends mens rea to be required for a criminal offence; it is displaced only by clear words or necessary implication.

House of Lords held that the marital exemption to rape was no longer part of English law. Shows the courts developing an existing offence; Strasbourg found no Article 7 breach (CR v UK; SW v UK (1995)).
The courts no longer have power to create new criminal offences; that is for Parliament.

Evidential burden: D must raise enough evidence to put a defence in issue; the prosecution must then disprove it. Legal burden: the party must prove the issue (D proves insanity on the balance of probabilities).
A railway gatekeeper who left the crossing gate open was guilty of manslaughter: a contractual duty can ground liability for omission, and it can extend to people other than the employer.
Taking in a vulnerable relative and then neglecting her can create a duty through voluntary assumption of care; failure to summon help led to manslaughter convictions.
D who accidentally creates a dangerous situation and then becomes aware of it is under a duty to take reasonable steps to counteract it (squatter, smouldering mattress, arson).

D who supplied heroin to her half-sister and realised she had overdosed owed a duty to seek help, because she had contributed to a life-threatening situation (Miller principle); gross negligence manslaughter.
D poisoned his mother, who died of an unrelated heart attack. No factual ('but for') causation, so guilty only of attempted murder.
Negligent medical treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent of D's acts, and so potent, that D's contribution becomes insignificant.
Thin skull rule: D must take V as he finds him, including V's religious beliefs. V's refusal of a transfusion did not break the chain.
The free, deliberate and informed decision of a fully informed adult to self-inject a drug breaks the chain; the supplier who handed over the syringe was not guilty of unlawful act manslaughter.
'Maliciously' in the 1861 Act means intention or subjective recklessness: D must have foreseen the risk of the harm and gone on to take it (gas meter case).
Introduced objective recklessness for criminal damage: creating an obvious risk and giving no thought to it. Overruled by R v G [2003].
Reckless as to a result if aware of a risk that it will occur (or, for a circumstance, that it exists or will exist) and it is, in the circumstances known to D, unreasonable to take that risk.
Two boys aged 11 and 12 set fire to newspapers behind a shop, expecting the fire to go out. It spread, causing about £1m damage. Convictions quashed as they did not appreciate the risk.

The Divisional Court overturned the acquittal of a 14-year-old girl with learning difficulties: under Caldwell she was reckless although the risk would not have been obvious to her. Cited in R v G as showing Caldwell's unfairness.
Transferred malice: D aimed a belt at one man and hit a woman. His mens rea transferred because the offence was of the same kind.
Malice does not transfer between different kinds of offence: intending to hit people does not supply mens rea for breaking a window.
No 'double transfer' of malice from mother to foetus to the later-born child for murder; unlawful act manslaughter was possible.
Without lawful excuse, destroying or damaging property belonging to another, intending or being reckless as to the destruction or damage.

cards.f: Hardman v CC of Avon and Somerset [1986]
cards.b: Water-soluble paint silhouettes were 'damage' because the council incurred cost and effort to remove them: temporary impairment can be enough.
An honest belief that the property is D's own negatives mens rea for s1(1), even if mistaken in law and unreasonable.
Lawful excuse if D believed the person entitled to consent had or would have consented. The belief need only be honestly held, not justified.
D's drunken but honest belief that her friend would consent to her breaking into what she thought was his house gave a s5(2)(a) defence, because s5(3) asks only whether the belief was honest.
For s5(2)(b), whether D acted 'in order to protect property' is judged objectively; acts aimed at a remote future risk fall outside it.
For aggravated criminal damage (s1(2)), the danger to life must arise from the damage to property, not from D's act causing it (bullets fired at windows).
Criminal damage (basic or aggravated) committed by fire; maximum life imprisonment.
Intentionally or recklessly causing V to apprehend immediate unlawful force. Summary offence charged under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988.
Intentionally or recklessly applying unlawful force to another, however slight. Can be indirect (Haystead v CC of Derbyshire [2000]).
Silent telephone calls can be an assault if they make V fear unlawful force within a short time; words or silence can suffice.
ABH can include a recognised clinical psychiatric condition, but not mere emotions such as fear, distress or panic.
Only the mens rea of the assault or battery; D need not intend or foresee ABH (R v Roberts (1971); R v Savage [1992]).
For s20, 'maliciously' requires D to intend or foresee the risk of some harm, though not serious harm.
A wound requires a break in both layers of the skin; internal bleeding from a ruptured blood vessel in the eye was not enough.
'Inflict' in s20 does not require an assault; a stalking campaign causing severe depressive illness could be inflicting GBH.
Consent is no defence where ABH is intended or caused in a street fight: it is not in the public interest for people to cause each other ABH for no good reason.
House of Lords (3-2): consent is no defence to ABH or wounding in sadomasochistic activity; no new exception created on public policy grounds.
A husband who branded his initials on his wife's buttocks at her request was not guilty; likened to tattooing, and consensual activity between spouses at home was not a proper matter for prosecution.
Injuries in contact sport are criminal only if sufficiently grave; factors include the sport, level, nature of the act, degree of force and D's state of mind.

cards.f: R v Dica [2004] / R v Konzani [2005]
cards.b: V can consent to the risk of an STI if the consent is informed; consent to sex is not consent to a concealed risk of infection, so D may be guilty under s20.
Consent no defence for a body modifier who removed an ear and nipple and split a tongue; the court refused to extend the tattooing exception.
For ss18, 20 and 47 OAPA, V's consent to serious harm for sexual gratification is not a defence (with a limited STI exception). Restates Brown and Emmett.
Women consented to breast examinations for medical purposes only; as D's purpose was not medical, they were deceived as to the nature or quality of the act, so there was no real consent.
Intention to kill or intention to cause grievous bodily harm (R v Vickers [1957]; R v Cunningham [1982]).
Direct intention: a decision to bring about the result, so far as it lies within D's power, whether or not D desired it.
Foresight of consequences is evidence from which intention may be inferred, not intention itself.
The jury is not entitled to find intention unless death or serious bodily harm was a virtual certainty (barring unforeseen intervention) and D appreciated this.
Woollin is a rule of evidence: foresight of virtual certainty allows, but does not require, the jury to find intention.

cards.f: Foetus as 'person in being' (A-G's Ref (No 3 of 1994))
cards.b: A foetus is not a 'person in being'; murder could not be founded on injury to the mother causing the later death of the born child. Manslaughter was possible.
Secondary liability requires intention to assist or encourage the crime; foresight that the principal might commit it is evidence of intention, not a substitute for it.

cards.f: Law Reform (Year and a Day Rule) Act 1996
cards.b: Abolished the rule that death must occur within a year and a day; the Attorney General's consent is required in some cases, e.g. death more than three years after injury.

Killing resulted from loss of self-control (need not be sudden); a qualifying trigger; and a person of D's sex and age with normal tolerance and self-restraint, in D's circumstances, might have reacted similarly.
Fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person; and/or circumstances of an extremely grave character causing a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged.
Sexual infidelity cannot be a qualifying trigger by itself (s55(6)(c)), but it may be considered as context where another trigger is relied on.

Abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition that substantially impaired D's ability to understand, form rational judgment or exercise self-control, and explains the killing. D proves it on balance of probabilities.
'Substantially impaired' means impairment that is important or weighty, not merely more than trivial.
An unlawful act is dangerous if all sober and reasonable people would inevitably recognise it must subject V to at least the risk of some harm.

cards.f: R v Dawson (1985) / R v Watson [1989]
cards.b: The reasonable person has the knowledge D had or would have gained: unknown heart condition (Dawson) versus obvious frailty of an elderly victim seen during a burglary (Watson). Both convictions were quashed, Watson's on causation.
Gross negligence manslaughter: duty, breach causing death, and negligence so bad the jury judges it criminal.
For gross negligence manslaughter, a serious and obvious risk of death must have been reasonably foreseeable at the time of breach, based on what D actually knew.
Dishonestly appropriating property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it.
An appropriation can occur even if the owner consents, including consent obtained by deception (dud cheques).
Receiving a gift that is valid in civil law can be an appropriation; dishonesty is the safeguard.
Not dishonest if D believes: (a) he has a legal right to deprive; (b) the owner would consent if he knew the circumstances; (c) the owner cannot be discovered by reasonable steps.

cards.f: Ivey v Genting [2017] / Barton and Booth [2020]
cards.b: Dishonesty: (1) find D's actual knowledge or belief as to the facts; (2) was the conduct dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people? No requirement that D realised this (Ghosh limb two gone).
Property 'belongs to' anyone in possession or control (s5(1)); an owner who took his car back from a garage without paying could steal it.
Under s5(4), overpaid wages remained 'property belonging to another' because there was a legal obligation to restore them.
Borrowing is theft only if equivalent to an outright taking, e.g. when the 'goodness, virtue and practical value' of the property is gone; films copied and returned were not stolen.
Confidential information (an exam paper's contents) is not 'property' under s4, so reading it is not theft.

cards.f: Three ways of committing fraud (s1 Fraud Act 2006)
cards.b: By false representation (s2), by failing to disclose information under a legal duty (s3), and by abuse of position (s4). Maximum 10 years.
If it is untrue or misleading, and D knows that it is, or might be, untrue or misleading.
Any representation as to fact or law, including as to the state of mind of D or another; may be express or implied (e.g. by conduct).
A representation is treated as made if submitted in any form to a system or device designed to receive or respond to communications, e.g. a card terminal or website.
No one needs to be deceived and no gain or loss need actually result; the offence is complete when D dishonestly acts with the required intention.
D occupies a position in which he is expected to safeguard, or not act against, another's financial interests and dishonestly abuses it (can be by omission), intending gain or loss.
Unlicensed gangmasters who controlled workers' wages and accommodation could occupy a position for s4; whether such a position exists is partly a jury question.
A result crime: D obtains services by a dishonest act, knowing payment is or might be required, intending not to pay in full.
An act done by the muscles without any control by the mind. Requires total loss of voluntary control from an external cause; leads to a complete acquittal.
Reduced or partial awareness ('driving without awareness') is not automatism; there must be total destruction of voluntary control.

cards.f: R v Quick [1973] v R v Hennessy [1989]
cards.b: Hypoglycaemia caused by insulin (external) is non-insane automatism; hyperglycaemia from failing to take insulin (the disease itself) is insanity.
D proves, on balance of probabilities, a defect of reason from disease of the mind such that he did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong.
'Wrong' in the M'Naghten Rules means both against the law and wrong by the standards of ordinary reasonable people.

cards.f: R v Sullivan [1984] / R v Burgess [1991]
cards.b: Epilepsy (Sullivan) and sleepwalking (Burgess) arise from internal causes and are 'diseases of the mind' in law, leading to the insanity verdict.
Voluntary intoxication may negate mens rea for specific intent offences but is no defence to basic intent offences.
Involuntary intoxication is no defence if D still formed the mens rea: a drugged intent is still an intent.
D cannot rely on a mistaken belief in the need for self-defence that was caused by voluntary intoxication.

cards.f: s76 Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008
cards.b: Self-defence: (1) did D genuinely believe force was necessary (judged on facts as D believed)? (2) was the force reasonable in those circumstances? Disproportionate force is not reasonable.
Force that is grossly disproportionate is never reasonable; disproportionate force may or may not be reasonable (R (Collins) v SSJ [2016]; R v Ray [2017]).
D is judged on the facts as he honestly believed them, and a person about to be attacked need not wait to be struck first.
Duress is unavailable if D voluntarily associated with criminals and ought reasonably to have foreseen the risk of being compelled by threats of violence.

Threat of death or serious injury to D, family or someone D reasonably feels responsible for; D must reasonably believe it is genuine and will be carried out immediately or almost immediately (Hasan).

cards.f: R v Howe [1987] / R v Gotts [1992]
cards.b: Duress is no defence to murder, whether as principal or accessory (Howe), or to attempted murder (Gotts).
Characteristics relevant to the reasonable firmness test include age, sex, pregnancy, serious physical disability and recognised psychiatric illness; low IQ alone does not lower the standard.
Necessity justified separating twins: needed to avoid inevitable and irreparable evil, no more than reasonably necessary, and not disproportionate. Limited to its facts.

questions.q: Dan accidentally reverses his car onto Pam's foot. When she tells him, he says 'You can wait' and switches off the engine for a minute. Which best explains why Dan can be convicted of battery?
options: He cannot be convicted because actus reus and mens rea must begin at exactly the same instant
Battery is a strict liability offence, so his state of mind is irrelevant
Battery requires actual bodily harm, which Pam suffered
Driving onto the foot and staying there was a continuing act, and his mens rea arose while it continued
questions.why: Fagan v MPC treats the car resting on the foot as a continuing act, so mens rea formed during it is enough. Battery is not strict liability: intention or recklessness as to applying force is required. Actual bodily harm is an element of the s47 offence, not of battery. The claim that both elements must begin at the same instant is the strict view that Fagan rejected.

questions.q: Which statement about the burden of proof in criminal trials in England and Wales is correct?
options: If D raises self-defence, D must prove it on the balance of probabilities
The prosecution must prove each element beyond reasonable doubt, but D bears the legal burden of proving insanity on the balance of probabilities
The prosecution must prove guilt on the balance of probabilities
D must disprove mens rea once the prosecution proves the actus reus
questions.why: Woolmington sets the general rule that the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and insanity is the classic common-law exception where D carries the legal burden. For self-defence D carries only an evidential burden, after which the prosecution must disprove it. The balance of probabilities is the civil standard. There is no general rule that D must disprove mens rea; that would reverse the golden thread.

questions.q: Explain the presumption of mens rea and when the courts will treat an offence as one of strict liability.
markScheme: States the presumption that mens rea is required (Sweet v Parsley [1970])
Notes the presumption is strong and can be displaced only by clear words or necessary implication (B v DPP [2000])
Identifies the Gammon [1985] factors: regulatory nature, public safety concern, whether strict liability promotes compliance
Gives an example or explains the rationale and criticism (e.g. convicting the morally blameless)
questions.modelAnswer:
The courts start from a presumption that Parliament intends a criminal offence to require mens rea, even if the statute is silent. In Sweet v Parsley [1970] a landlady who did not know that tenants were smoking cannabis on her premises was not guilty of being "concerned in the management" of premises used for that purpose; the House of Lords read in a mental element. In B v DPP [2000] the House of Lords held that the presumption is displaced only by express words or necessary implication, and that a genuine belief that a child was over 14 negated mens rea for the offence charged.

The presumption is most readily displaced for regulatory offences. Gammon (Hong Kong) v A-G [1985] identified relevant factors: whether the offence is "truly criminal" or regulatory, whether it deals with an issue of social concern such as public safety, and whether strict liability would encourage greater vigilance. Strict liability is defended on grounds of efficiency and protection of the public, but criticised because it can convict people who were not at fault.

questions.q: Kim prepares a syringe of heroin and hands it to her friend Lee, an adult who knows what it is. Lee injects himself and dies. Kim is charged with unlawful act manslaughter. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Not guilty, because Lee's free, deliberate and informed self-injection broke the chain of causation
Guilty, because supplying a controlled drug is an unlawful act that was a 'but for' cause of death
Guilty, because under Blaue Kim must take her victim as she finds him
Not guilty, because manslaughter can never be committed by someone who supplies drugs
questions.why: Kennedy (No 2) holds that a fully informed adult's free and deliberate act of self-injection is a new intervening act, so the supplier did not cause the death. Supply being an unlawful act and a 'but for' cause is not enough without legal causation. The thin skull rule in Blaue concerns the victim's pre-existing conditions and beliefs, not a voluntary act that itself causes death. The claim that a supplier can never be liable goes too far: Evans shows a supplier can be guilty of gross negligence manslaughter by omission if a duty to seek help arises.

questions.q: Sam falls asleep holding a lit cigarette. He wakes to find his mattress smouldering, moves to another room and goes back to sleep. The house is damaged by fire. Why can Sam be liable for arson?
options: Because he was reckless when the cigarette fell from his hand
Because a householder has a contractual duty to the insurer to prevent fires
He cannot be liable, as English law never imposes criminal liability for omissions
Because, having created a dangerous situation and become aware of it, he was under a duty to take reasonable steps to deal with it
questions.why: This is R v Miller: liability rests on a duty arising from D's creation of the danger, breached when he became aware of it and did nothing. He was asleep when the cigarette fell, so there was no mens rea at that moment. No contractual duty to an insurer is involved. English law does impose liability for omissions where a duty exists, so the statement that it never does is wrong.

questions.q: When will negligent medical treatment break the chain of causation between D's injury and V's death? Refer to case law.
markScheme: States the test of legal causation: D's act must be an operating and more than minimal cause
R v Smith [1959]: original wound still operating and substantial despite poor treatment
R v Cheshire [1991]: treatment breaks the chain only if so independent and potent that D's contribution is insignificant
R v Jordan (1956) as an exceptional case where the wound had largely healed and treatment was palpably wrong
Malcherek and Steel [1981]: switching off life support does not break the chain
questions.modelAnswer: D's conduct must be a legal cause of death: an operating cause that contributes more than minimally, though it need not be the sole cause. The courts are very reluctant to let medical treatment break the chain. In R v Smith [1959] a soldier who had been stabbed was dropped twice and given poor treatment, but the stab wound was still "an operating cause and a substantial cause", so D was liable. In R v Cheshire [1991] the Court of Appeal held that even negligent treatment breaks the chain only where it is so independent of D's acts, and so potent in causing death, that D's contribution can be regarded as insignificant; there V died of a rare complication from a tracheotomy while his gunshot wounds were no longer life-threatening, but D was still liable. R v Jordan (1956), where the stab wound had mainly healed and the treatment was "palpably wrong", is treated as exceptional. Finally, switching off life support after brain-stem death does not break the chain (Malcherek and Steel [1981]).

questions.q: Two children aged 11 and 12 set fire to some papers in a yard, expecting the fire to burn out. It spreads to a building. Following R v G [2003], what must the prosecution prove for recklessness?
options: That each child was aware of a risk of damage to property and that, in the circumstances known to them, it was unreasonable to take it
That each child foresaw damage as virtually certain
That the risk of damage would have been obvious to a reasonable adult
That the risk would have been obvious to a reasonable child of the same age
questions.why: R v G adopted a subjective test: awareness of the risk by D, plus unreasonableness of taking it. The 'reasonable adult' test is Caldwell, which R v G overruled. The House of Lords also declined to modify Caldwell to a reasonable person of the child's age, preferring a subjective test. Virtual certainty is the Woollin test for oblique intention, a higher standard than recklessness.

questions.q: Tom throws a stone at Vic, intending to hit him. He misses and breaks a shop window. What is the position on criminal damage?
options: Tom is guilty because criminal damage is an offence of strict liability
Malice does not transfer from an offence against the person to property, so Tom is guilty only if he was himself reckless as to damaging property
Tom is guilty, because intending to commit any offence transfers to whatever harm results (Latimer)
Tom cannot be guilty of criminal damage in any circumstances because he aimed at a person
questions.why: Pembliton shows that transferred malice works only within the same kind of offence, but Tom can still be liable if he personally foresaw a risk of damaging property (R v G recklessness). Latimer involved the same type of offence against a different victim, so it does not support transfer from person to property. Saying he can never be guilty ignores his own possible recklessness. Criminal damage requires intention or recklessness, so it is not strict liability.

questions.q: Why did the House of Lords in R v G [2003] overrule MPC v Caldwell [1982]?
markScheme: States the Caldwell test (obvious risk, no thought given)
States the R v G test (awareness of risk and unreasonable to take it)
Reason: conviction for serious crime should require a culpable state of mind
Reason: Caldwell misinterpreted Parliament's intention in the Criminal Damage Act 1971
Reason: unfairness to children and those of limited capacity (Elliott v C) and widespread criticism
questions.modelAnswer: In Caldwell the House of Lords held that D was reckless for criminal damage if he created an obvious risk of damage and either gave no thought to it or recognised it and took it anyway. "Obvious" meant obvious to a reasonable prudent person, not to D. In R v G [2003], where two young boys started a fire that they expected to burn out, the House of Lords overruled Caldwell and held that D is reckless only if aware of the risk and it is unreasonable, in the circumstances known to D, to take it. Lord Bingham gave several reasons. First, conviction for a serious crime should depend on proof that D had a culpable state of mind; it is not enough that D's conduct fell below an objective standard. Second, Caldwell misinterpreted the Criminal Damage Act 1971, which was intended to keep the subjective approach to "maliciously" found in Cunningham. Third, the objective test produced obvious unfairness, as in Elliott v C, where a 14-year-old girl with learning difficulties was held to be reckless although the risk would not have been obvious to her. Fourth, the decision had been heavily criticised by academics and judges, and was not one the House could leave in place.

questions.q: Jo, very drunk, breaks the window of a house to get in, believing it is her friend's house and that he would not mind. It is a stranger's house. Charged under s1(1) CDA 1971, which is correct?
options: She has a lawful excuse only if the actual owner would have consented
She has a lawful excuse under s5(2)(a), because s5(3) requires only an honest belief, even if caused by intoxication
She has no defence, because voluntary intoxication cannot be relied on for a basic intent offence
She has a lawful excuse only if her belief was reasonable
questions.why: Jaggard v Dickinson held that the statutory wording of s5(3) protects any honestly held belief, including a drunken one. The general Majewski rule on intoxication does not override this specific statutory defence. Section 5(3) says the belief need not be justified, so reasonableness is not required. The defence depends on D's belief, not on what the actual owner would have done.

questions.q: Ron fires a shotgun through the window of an occupied house. Nobody is hurt. He is charged with aggravated criminal damage under s1(2). What must the prosecution prove about danger to life?
options: Nothing, because firing a gun at a house is automatically aggravated criminal damage
That someone's life was actually endangered by the pellets
That Ron intended or was reckless as to whether life would be endangered by the damage to the property, such as flying glass
That someone was physically injured
questions.why: Steer requires the intended or foreseen danger to life to come from the damage itself, such as shattered glass, so Ron's state of mind about that damage is the issue. Danger from the pellets is exactly what Steer held to be insufficient, and in any case actual endangerment is not required because the offence turns on D's intention or recklessness. Injury is not an element of s1(2). Nothing is automatic: the mens rea about endangering life by the damage must be proved.

questions.q: Explain what counts as 'damage' under the Criminal Damage Act 1971, with authority.
markScheme: Damage is a question of fact and degree
Includes impairment of value or usefulness, including temporary impairment needing cost or effort to remedy (Hardman)
Trivial marks that can be wiped off without cost may not be damage (A (a juvenile) v R)
Applies the idea to an example, e.g. graffiti or removable paint
questions.modelAnswer: Damage is not defined in the Act and is a question of fact and degree for the tribunal. It is not limited to permanent physical harm: property is damaged if its value or usefulness is impaired, even temporarily, particularly where removing the effect costs time or money. In Hardman v Chief Constable of Avon and Somerset [1986] protesters painted silhouettes on a pavement in water-soluble paint that rain would eventually have washed away; because the council paid to have it removed, it was damage. By contrast, in A (a juvenile) v R [1978] spitting on a police officer's raincoat was not damage because it could simply be wiped off and left no lasting effect. Graffiti that requires professional cleaning is therefore likely to be damage, whereas a mark removed with a tissue probably is not.

questions.q: Ann throws a glass of beer at Bea, intending only to soak her. The glass slips from her hand and cuts Bea's wrist. Ann did not foresee any injury. What is Ann's most serious likely liability?
options: Wounding with intent under s18, because a wound was caused
Assault occasioning ABH under s47, because she intended a battery and ABH resulted
Malicious wounding under s20, because the cut broke the skin
Battery only, because ABH must be foreseen
questions.why: On these facts (as in R v Savage) s47 needs only the mens rea for battery, so the cut makes it s47. Section 18 requires intention to cause GBH, which Ann lacked. Section 20 requires foresight of some harm (Mowatt), and Ann foresaw none, so a wound alone is not enough. The idea that ABH must be foreseen for s47 was rejected in Roberts and Savage.

questions.q: Which statement about psychiatric injury and the OAPA 1861 is correct?
options: A recognised clinical psychiatric condition can be ABH or GBH, but fear or distress alone is not bodily harm
Psychiatric harm can never be bodily harm because the Act refers only to the body
Any emotional distress caused by D counts as ABH
Only GBH, not ABH, can take the form of psychiatric injury
questions.why: Chan-Fook and Ireland/Burstow treat recognised psychiatric illness as bodily harm at both levels, while excluding mere emotions. The idea that 'bodily' excludes the mind was the argument the courts rejected. Ordinary distress is expressly excluded by Chan-Fook. There is no rule confining psychiatric injury to GBH: Chan-Fook itself concerned ABH.

questions.q: Distinguish the offences under s20 and s18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861.
markScheme: s20: unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting GBH; maximum 5 years
s20 mens rea: intention or recklessness as to some harm (Mowatt; Parmenter)
s18: wounding or causing GBH with intent to do GBH (or to resist or prevent lawful arrest); maximum life
s18 requires specific intention (Woollin meaning); recklessness is not enough
'Cause' in s18 is wider than 'inflict' in s20, though Burstow narrowed the gap
questions.modelAnswer: Both offences share the same harms: a wound (a break in both layers of skin, JCC v Eisenhower) or grievous bodily harm (really serious harm, DPP v Smith). The key difference is mens rea. For s20, "maliciously" requires only that D intended or foresaw the risk of some harm, not serious harm (R v Mowatt; DPP v Parmenter). This makes s20 a partly constructive offence, and its maximum sentence is 5 years. Section 18 requires D to act with intent to do GBH or, where D wounds or causes GBH, with intent to resist or prevent lawful apprehension. Intention has its Woollin meaning, so recklessness is not enough. Section 18 is far more serious, with a maximum of life imprisonment. The verbs also differ: s18 uses "cause", which covers any causal contribution, while s20 uses "inflict". After R v Burstow, "inflict" does not need an assault, so the practical difference is now small.

questions.q: Kai, a body modification artist, removes Lou's ear at Lou's sincere and informed request. Lou suffers no complications. Is Lou's consent a defence to a charge of wounding?
options: No, because consent can only be a defence if a doctor carries out the procedure
No, because the courts have refused to extend the recognised exceptions to body modification of this kind
Yes, because the tattooing exception covers any cosmetic procedure carried out by a professional
Yes, because s71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 bars consent only where harm is for sexual gratification, so consent is otherwise always a defence
questions.why: R v BM held that removing body parts is not within the tattooing or piercing exception, and the court declined to create a new one. Wilson's adornment reasoning does not stretch to every cosmetic procedure. Section 71 states expressly that it does not change the law on other situations, so it does not make consent a general defence elsewhere. There is no rule that only a doctor can rely on consent: tattooists and piercers can, within the recognised categories.

questions.q: Dev knows he has HIV but does not tell his partner Eve. They have unprotected sex and Eve is infected. Which is correct?
options: Dev can be guilty of inflicting GBH under s20, because Eve did not give informed consent to the risk of infection
Dev cannot be guilty because consent to sex covers all its risks
Dev cannot be guilty because transmitting a disease is not 'inflicting' harm
Dev is guilty under s18 because infection is always intended GBH
questions.why: Dica and Konzani hold that consent to sexual intercourse is not consent to a concealed risk of infection, so an s20 conviction is possible if Dev was at least reckless as to transmission. The idea that consent to sex covers every risk was rejected in those cases.
