Dica held that the old view in R v Clarence (1888), that infection cannot be 'inflicted', no longer applies to s20; Clarence was not formally overruled, but Ireland and Burstow had removed its foundations. Section 18 requires proof of intention to cause GBH, which is not presumed.

questions.q: 'R v Brown [1994] is an unjustified intrusion into personal autonomy.' Briefly evaluate this claim.
markScheme: Outlines Brown: 3-2 majority, consent no defence to ABH or wounding in sadomasochistic activity
Majority reasoning: public interest, risk of escalation, infection, corruption of young people
Minority reasoning: autonomy, privacy (Article 8), law should intervene only where serious harm
Contrasts Wilson [1997] and the sports or horseplay exceptions as inconsistent or explained on policy grounds
Notes s71 Domestic Abuse Act 2021 now places the Brown position on a statutory footing for sexual gratification
Reaches a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
In Brown a group of men engaged in consensual sadomasochistic acts causing wounds and ABH. The majority held that consent is no defence to ABH or worse unless the activity falls within an established exception, and refused to create one for sadomasochism. They relied on public interest arguments: the risk that activities could escalate, the danger of infection and the possible corruption of young men. The minority (Lords Mustill and Slynn) argued that adults' private consensual conduct should not be criminalised unless there is a good reason, and that the 1861 Act was not designed for this situation.

The claim has force. The exceptions recognised elsewhere look inconsistent: rough horseplay and contact sports allow serious injury, and in Wilson branding was lawful because it was compared to tattooing, while the Brown men were convicted for comparable injuries. Critics argue the decision reflects moral disapproval rather than harm. On the other hand, the courts have drawn a line at serious harm, and the policy concerns about escalation are real; in Emmett and BM, the courts were dealing with risks of serious injury. Parliament has also endorsed the Brown approach in s71 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, which removes consent as a defence to serious harm for sexual gratification. The best view may be that Brown is defensible as policy on serious harm but that the boundaries of the exceptions are poorly explained.

questions.q: Which is the correct direction on oblique intention following R v Woollin [1999]?
options: The jury is not entitled to find intention unless death or serious harm was virtually certain and D appreciated this
The jury must find intention if D foresaw death or serious harm as virtually certain
The jury may infer intention whenever death was a natural consequence of D's act
Foresight of death as highly probable is sufficient for intention
questions.why: Woollin states that the jury is not entitled to find intention unless both conditions are met, and Matthews and Alleyne confirms that the jury then may, but need not, find intention. Saying the jury must find it treats foresight as intention itself, which Matthews and Alleyne rejected. The 'natural consequence' wording comes from Moloney and was later found misleading. 'Highly probable' foresight reflects the older approach in Hyam, which is not enough after Nedrick and Woollin.

questions.q: Dan beats Vic intending to break both his legs but not to kill him. Vic dies of his injuries. What is Dan's likely liability?
options: Murder, because an intention to cause grievous bodily harm is sufficient malice aforethought
Manslaughter only, because Dan did not intend to kill
Murder only if Dan foresaw death as virtually certain
Wounding with intent under s18 only, because death was not intended
questions.why: Vickers and Cunningham confirm that intention to cause GBH is enough for murder, and breaking both legs is really serious harm. The belief that murder needs an intention to kill is a common error. Virtual certainty of death is relevant only to proving oblique intention, not where GBH is D's direct aim. Section 18 would be the charge if Vic survived, but because death resulted, the homicide offence applies.

questions.q: Trace the development of the law on oblique intention from Moloney to Woollin, and explain the effect of Matthews and Alleyne.
markScheme: Moloney [1985]: foresight is evidence of intention; natural consequence guidelines
Hancock and Shankland [1986]: Moloney guidelines defective; probability relevant
Nedrick [1986]: virtual certainty test ('infer')
Woollin [1999]: approved Nedrick, substituted 'find'; murder conviction quashed
Matthews and Alleyne [2003]: rule of evidence, jury may but need not find intention
Comment on remaining uncertainty or moral elbow-room
questions.modelAnswer: Oblique intention concerns results that are not D's purpose but are side effects of what he does. In Moloney [1985] the House of Lords held that foresight is evidence of intention rather than intention itself, and suggested asking whether death was a natural consequence of D's act and whether D foresaw this. In Hancock and Shankland [1986], where striking miners dropped a concrete block onto a taxi, the House of Lords said the Moloney guidelines were defective because they did not mention probability; the more probable the consequence, the more likely it was foreseen and intended. In Nedrick [1986] the Court of Appeal gave a model direction: the jury was not entitled to infer intention unless death or serious harm was a virtual certainty as a result of D's actions and D appreciated this. In Woollin [1999] the House of Lords approved Nedrick but replaced "infer" with "find", and quashed a murder conviction where the judge had used a lower "substantial risk" test. In Matthews and Alleyne [2003] the Court of Appeal held that Woollin sets a rule of evidence: once the conditions are met the jury may find intention, but is not obliged to. This leaves the jury some moral discretion, which promotes just outcomes but at the cost of certainty.

questions.q: Mia kills her partner after discovering that he has been having an affair. There is no other provocation or fear. Is the loss of control defence likely to succeed?
options: Yes, if Mia proves on the balance of probabilities that a normal person might have done the same
Yes, because discovering infidelity is a circumstance of an extremely grave character
No, because the loss of self-control was not sudden
No, because sexual infidelity must be disregarded as a qualifying trigger and there is no other trigger
questions.why: Section 55(6)(c) requires sexual infidelity to be disregarded, and Clinton allows it only as context for another trigger, which is absent here. Treating infidelity itself as an extremely grave circumstance is what s55(6)(c) excludes. Section 54(2) says the loss of control need not be sudden, so that is not the reason for failure. D bears only an evidential burden for loss of control; the prosecution must then disprove it, so a legal burden on Mia is wrong.

questions.q: During a robbery, two masked men threaten a petrol station attendant with a replica gun. Unknown to them, he has a serious heart condition, and he dies of a heart attack. What is the key issue for unlawful act manslaughter?
options: Nothing more needs to be shown, because robbery is an unlawful act and death resulted
Whether a sober and reasonable person with the robbers' knowledge would have recognised the risk of some physical harm
Nothing more needs to be shown, because the thin skull rule makes any unlawful act dangerous
Whether the robbers themselves foresaw some harm to the attendant
questions.why: Dawson, on similar facts, held that the sober and reasonable person knows only what D knew, and the convictions were quashed because the jury had not been properly directed that such a person must have recognised a risk of some physical harm. The thin skull rule is about causation, not whether the act was dangerous. Newbury held that D need not personally foresee harm, so the robbers' own foresight is not the test. An unlawful act causing death is not enough by itself, because the Church dangerousness requirement must also be met.

questions.q: Set out the elements of gross negligence manslaughter after R v Adomako and R v Rose.
markScheme: Duty of care, using ordinary negligence principles
Breach of that duty causing death (causation to criminal standard: Broughton)
Serious and obvious risk of death reasonably foreseeable at time of breach, based on D's actual knowledge (Rose)
Breach so bad that the jury considers it criminal (Adomako)
Comment on circularity criticism or role of the jury
questions.modelAnswer: Gross negligence manslaughter was restated by the House of Lords in R v Adomako [1995], where an anaesthetist failed for several minutes to notice that the patient's oxygen tube had become disconnected. First, D must owe V a duty of care, decided on ordinary negligence principles. Second, D must breach that duty. Third, it must have been reasonably foreseeable that the breach gave rise to a serious and obvious risk of death, not merely of serious injury. In R v Rose [2017] the Court of Appeal held that this is judged at the time of breach and by reference to what D actually knew, not what D would have known had the duty been performed; an optometrist who failed to examine a child's eyes properly was therefore not guilty, as she did not know of the abnormality. Fourth, the breach must cause death, proved beyond reasonable doubt (R v Broughton [2020]). Finally, the jury must decide that the negligence was so bad as to be criminal. Critics say this last step is circular, since the jury is told a crime is committed if it thinks the conduct criminal.

questions.q: Dee takes boxes of pens from her employer's stockroom for her children's school. She knows company policy forbids this, but thinks 'everyone does it' and sees nothing wrong. Ordinary decent people would regard it as dishonest. Applying Ivey and Barton and Booth, which is correct?
options: She is not dishonest under s2(1)(b) because she believed her employer would consent
Dishonesty is a question of law for the judge, who must decide whether her belief was reasonable
She is dishonest: her actual beliefs about the facts are taken into account, but the standard is that of ordinary decent people
She is not dishonest because she did not realise ordinary decent people would regard her conduct as dishonest
questions.why: Under Ivey, confirmed for criminal law in Barton and Booth, the jury finds D's genuine beliefs about the facts and then applies the objective standard, ignoring D's own view of what is honest. The requirement that D realised others would think it dishonest was Ghosh's second limb, which no longer applies. Section 2(1)(b) does not help because Dee knew the employer forbade it, so she did not believe it would consent. Dishonesty is a question of fact for the jury, and reasonableness of a belief is only evidence of whether it was genuinely held.

questions.q: Han persuades Pat, a vulnerable but legally competent man, to give her £60,000. The gift is valid in civil law. Can Han be guilty of theft?
options: Yes: receiving a valid gift can be appropriation, and whether she was dishonest is for the jury
No, because there is no appropriation where the owner consents
Only if Pat lacked capacity to make the gift
No, because once the gift was valid the money belonged to Han
questions.why: R v Hinks held that acceptance of a valid gift can be appropriation of property belonging to another, leaving dishonesty to protect against unfair convictions. The argument that the money had become Han's was put by the dissent in Hinks and rejected by the majority, because the property belonged to Pat at the moment of appropriation. Lawrence and Gomez established that consent does not prevent appropriation. Lack of capacity is not required; in Hinks the jury did not need to find that the donor was incapable.

questions.q: Explain the meaning of 'intention of permanently depriving' in s6 of the Theft Act 1968.
markScheme: s6(1): treating the property as one's own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights
Borrowing or lending only if for a period and in circumstances equivalent to an outright taking
R v Lloyd [1985]: goodness, virtue and practical value test
Examples: ransom-type demands (Raphael [2008]); replacing money with equivalent (Velumyl)
Conditional intention / application to facts
questions.modelAnswer: Section 1 requires an intention of permanently depriving the other of the property, and s6 extends this. Under s6(1) D is regarded as having that intention if he intends to treat the thing as his own to dispose of regardless of the other's rights, even if he does not mean the owner to lose it permanently. In R v Raphael [2008] taking a car and demanding money for its return fell within s6(1), because D was treating it as his own to dispose of. Borrowing or lending counts only if it is for a period and in circumstances making it equivalent to an outright taking or disposal. In R v Lloyd [1985] a cinema projectionist lent films to be copied and returned them within hours; this was not theft because the films kept their "goodness, virtue and practical value". By contrast, borrowing a season ticket until it expires would qualify. Finally, taking cash intending to replace it later with equivalent notes is an intention to deprive the owner permanently of those specific notes (R v Velumyl [1989]).

questions.q: Sid uses a stolen bank card at a supermarket self-checkout to pay for groceries. Which statement is correct?
options: He commits fraud by false representation, because a representation to a device counts under s2(5)
He commits only theft of the card, because using a card makes no representation
He commits no fraud because a machine cannot be deceived
He commits fraud only if a cashier later checks the transaction
questions.why: Section 2(5) treats a representation submitted to a system or device as made, so using the card implies a false representation of authority (as Lambie shows under the old law). The idea that machines cannot be deceived was a problem under the old deception offences, which the 2006 Act was designed to solve. No human involvement is needed. Using a card does make an implied representation of authority to use it, so the claim that it makes none is wrong.

questions.q: Which statement about fraud by false representation under s2 of the Fraud Act 2006 is correct?
options: The offence can be complete even if nobody is deceived and nothing is gained or lost
D must actually make a gain or cause a loss
D must know the representation is definitely untrue; awareness that it might be untrue is not enough
A representation about D's own intentions cannot count
questions.why: Fraud is a conduct offence: making a false representation dishonestly, with intent to gain or cause loss, is enough. Section 2(1) requires only intention to make a gain or cause loss, not actual gain or loss. Section 2(2) is satisfied if D knows the statement is or might be untrue or misleading. Section 2(3) expressly includes representations as to a person's state of mind.

questions.q: Compare fraud by false representation (s2) with fraud by abuse of position (s4).
markScheme: Both require dishonesty (Ivey) and intention to make a gain or cause loss (s5)
s2 requires a false representation, express or implied, D knowing it is or might be false
s4 requires a position in which D is expected to safeguard another's financial interests, and abuse of it
s4 can be committed by omission; no representation needed (Valujevs on positions)
Both are conduct offences; no deception or actual loss needed
questions.modelAnswer:
Both are forms of the single offence of fraud under s1 of the Fraud Act 2006 and share core requirements. D must act dishonestly, judged by the Ivey test confirmed in Barton and Booth, and must intend to make a gain or cause a loss (or expose another to a risk of loss) in money or other property, as defined in s5. Both are conduct offences, so no one needs to be deceived and no loss need actually occur.

They differ in the conduct element. Section 2 requires a false representation as to fact, law or a state of mind, which can be express or implied, and D must know it is or might be untrue or misleading. Section 4 requires no representation at all. Instead D must occupy a position in which he is expected to safeguard, or not to act against, the financial interests of another, and dishonestly abuse that position, which may be done by omission. Typical examples are employees, trustees and company directors, and Valujevs [2014] shows the category can extend further, for example to gangmasters controlling workers' pay. Section 4 is therefore useful where D exploits a relationship of trust without saying anything false.

questions.q: Val has diabetes. She fails to take her insulin, becomes hyperglycaemic and, while confused, hits a nurse. Which plea is most likely to be available?
options: Insanity, because her condition arose from an internal cause, the diabetes itself
Non-insane automatism, because diabetes is a physical not a mental illness
No plea at all, because any condition linked to medication is self-induced
Involuntary intoxication, because insulin is a drug
questions.why: Hennessy held that hyperglycaemia from not taking insulin stems from the disease itself, an internal factor, so it falls within the M'Naghten Rules. 'Disease of the mind' is a legal test, so a physical illness affecting the mind counts, which is why non-insane automatism is wrong. Self-induced automatism (Bailey) concerns cases like failing to eat after taking insulin, and even then it is a defence to basic intent crimes unless D was reckless. Val took no insulin, so there is no intoxication at all.

questions.q: Ben is extremely drunk after a night out. He stabs Cal, who dies. The jury is not sure Ben formed an intention to kill or cause GBH. What is the likely outcome?
options: Guilty of murder, because voluntary intoxication is never relevant
Complete acquittal, because he lacked mens rea
Guilty of murder unless he can show the intoxication was involuntary
Not guilty of murder, but guilty of manslaughter
questions.why: Under Majewski, voluntary intoxication can be used to show lack of the specific intent required for murder, but manslaughter is a basic intent offence, so Ben is convicted of that (as in Lipman). Saying intoxication is never relevant ignores its role for specific intent crimes. An outright acquittal ignores the basic intent rule for manslaughter. Murder requires proof of intent, and the prosecution has failed to prove it here, whatever caused the intoxication; Kingston concerns D who did form the intent while involuntarily intoxicated.

questions.q: Explain the distinction between insane and non-insane automatism and evaluate it.
markScheme: Automatism: total loss of voluntary control; complete acquittal
Insanity under M'Naghten: disease of the mind is a legal concept; internal cause
Cases: Quick (external) v Hennessy (internal); Sullivan; Burgess; Kemp
Consequences: special verdict and disposals under 1964 Act; burden on D
Criticisms: arbitrary results, stigma, medical irrelevance
Reform suggestions (e.g. Law Commission 2013 discussion paper) or conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Automatism denies that D acted voluntarily. If the loss of control has an external cause, such as a blow to the head or an insulin injection, it is non-insane automatism and D is acquitted (R v Quick [1973]). If it results from an internal cause, it is a "disease of the mind" under the M'Naghten Rules and the verdict is not guilty by reason of insanity. "Disease of the mind" is a legal test: it has covered arteriosclerosis (Kemp), epilepsy (Sullivan), hyperglycaemia (Hennessy) and sleepwalking (Burgess). For insanity, D bears the legal burden on the balance of probabilities, and the court may impose a hospital order, a supervision order or an absolute discharge.

The distinction is widely criticised. It produces arbitrary results: a diabetic who takes too much insulin may be acquitted, while one who takes too little is "insane". It stigmatises people with epilepsy or diabetes, who may plead guilty rather than accept the label. It does not track whether D is dangerous: the internal cause test was designed to protect the public from recurring conditions, but a single external event can also recur. In a 2013 discussion paper the Law Commission provisionally proposed replacing the rules with a special defence of 'not criminally responsible by reason of a recognised medical condition', available where such a condition caused a total lack of capacity to form a rational judgement, to understand that the conduct was wrong, or to control one's actions; the proposals have not been taken forward. Overall the distinction serves public protection but at the price of coherence and fairness.

questions.q: Gil joins a drug gang knowing its members use violence. Later the gang leader threatens to kill him unless he carries drugs. Can Gil rely on duress?
options: Yes, because the threat was of death
No, but only if he actually foresaw being forced to commit this particular type of offence
No, because he voluntarily associated with criminals when he ought reasonably to have foreseen being compelled by threats of violence
No, because duress is never a defence to drug offences
questions.why: Hasan holds that duress is excluded where D voluntarily associated with people he ought reasonably to have foreseen might compel him by threats of violence. A threat of death meets one requirement, but it does not cure the voluntary association bar. Hasan made the test objective and rejected the need for D to foresee being forced to commit a particular type of offence. Duress is excluded only for murder and attempted murder, not drug offences.

questions.q: Hal, a householder, finds a burglar in his kitchen at night and, believing he is under attack, strikes him with a heavy object. The force is disproportionate but not grossly disproportionate. What follows?
options: The jury must decide whether the force was reasonable in the circumstances as Hal believed them to be
The defence fails because Hal could have retreated to another room
The force is automatically reasonable because it was not grossly disproportionate
The force is automatically unreasonable because any disproportionate force is unreasonable
questions.why: Collins and Ray hold that in householder cases grossly disproportionate force is never reasonable, but force short of that may or may not be reasonable, so the jury decides. Reading s76(5A) as making such force automatically reasonable was the interpretation the Divisional Court rejected. The rule that disproportionate force is unreasonable applies in non-householder cases under s76(6), but s76(5A) displaces it here. There is no duty to retreat; the possibility of retreat is only a factor under s76(6A).

questions.q: Why is duress not a defence to murder? Evaluate the law.
markScheme: States the rule: R v Howe [1987] (murder, including secondary parties); R v Gotts [1992] (attempted murder)
Reasoning: sanctity of life; ordinary person expected to sacrifice own life rather than kill innocent
Reasoning: risk of abuse by terrorists or gangs; executive discretion and sentencing
Criticism: law cannot demand heroism; inconsistency with attempted murder/GBH (s18) position historically
Criticism: mandatory life sentence means no mitigation; Law Commission proposals for duress as full or partial defence
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
In R v Howe [1987] the House of Lords held that duress is no defence to murder, whether D is the principal or a secondary party, and in R v Gotts [1992] extended the bar to attempted murder. The main reasoning is moral: the law should not permit an ordinary person to take an innocent life to save his own, because every life is equally valuable. Their Lordships were also concerned that a defence could be exploited by terrorists and gang leaders who coerce others, and argued that hard cases could be dealt with by the decision whether to prosecute.

The rule is open to criticism. Duress is usually seen as an excuse, not a justification: it does not say the act was right, only that D should not be blamed because a person of reasonable firmness would have done the same. Demanding heroism from defendants under a threat of death seems harsh, especially for secondary parties who play a minor role. Because murder carries a mandatory life sentence, D's situation cannot be reflected in the sentence. There are also oddities: duress was available for s18 GBH with intent, yet if V then dies D becomes guilty of murder with no defence. The Law Commission (Law Com No 304, 2006) recommended that duress should be a full defence to murder and attempted murder, subject to strict conditions: a threat of death or life-threatening harm, no realistic chance of seeking police protection, and the burden of proving the defence on D. On balance, the absolute bar is defensible as policy, but a partial defence reducing murder to manslaughter would better reflect D's reduced blameworthiness.

questions.q: Problem question. Ravi's neighbour Sam has threatened him for months. Last week Sam told him, 'Next time I see you, I'll put you in hospital.' One evening Sam comes towards Ravi in the street, shouting and swinging a bicycle chain. Ravi, terrified, pulls a kitchen knife from his shopping bag and stabs Sam once in the abdomen. Ravi later says he meant 'to stop him, whatever it took.' Sam is taken to hospital, where a junior doctor fails for several hours to notice internal bleeding. Sam dies. Medical evidence is that prompt treatment would probably have saved him, but the stab wound remained the medical cause of death. Discuss Ravi's criminal liability for Sam's death.
markScheme: Actus reus of murder: unlawful killing of a person in being; factual causation (but for)
Legal causation: medical negligence unlikely to break chain (Smith [1959]; Cheshire [1991]; Jordan distinguished)
Mens rea: intention to kill or cause GBH (Vickers); direct intention to cause GBH likely; Woollin if needed
Self-defence: genuine belief in need for force (subjective; Williams (Gladstone); Beckford); not a householder case
Reasonableness of force in circumstances as D believed them (s76 CJIA 2008, s76(6)-(7)); no duty to retreat (s76(6A)); complete acquittal if successful
If self-defence fails: loss of control (s54-55 CJA 2009): loss of self-control, fear of serious violence trigger, normal person test; not considered revenge
Burden: evidential on D, prosecution must disprove both defences; outcome voluntary manslaughter if loss of control applies
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Actus reus and causation. Ravi stabbed Sam, who died; but for the stabbing he would not have died. The issue is whether the doctor's failure to notice the bleeding broke the chain. In R v Smith [1959] poor medical treatment did not break the chain because the stab wound was still "an operating and substantial cause", and in R v Cheshire [1991] the Court of Appeal held that negligent treatment breaks the chain only where it is so independent and so potent that D's contribution becomes insignificant. Here the stab wound remained the medical cause of death, unlike R v Jordan (1956), where the wound had almost healed. Ravi legally caused Sam's death.

Mens rea. Murder requires intention to kill or to cause GBH (Vickers; Cunningham). Ravi's words "whatever it took" and the use of a knife to the abdomen strongly suggest at least a direct intention to cause really serious harm. If the jury doubted this, it could find oblique intention under Woollin only if death or serious harm was a virtual certainty and Ravi appreciated that, which is likely for a stab to the abdomen. The mens rea for murder is probably present.

Self-defence. Ravi will argue self-defence under common law as clarified by s76 Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008. First, did he genuinely believe force was necessary? This is judged on the facts as he believed them (Williams (Gladstone); Beckford). Given the threats and the chain, a genuine belief is very likely, and he need not wait to be struck. Second, was the force reasonable in the circumstances as he believed them? A single stab against a man swinging a chain may well be seen as reasonable: Ravi had to react in the heat of the moment, and s76(7) says an honest and instinctive response is strong evidence of reasonableness. The possibility of retreat is only a factor (s76(6A)). This is not a householder case, so disproportionate force would defeat the defence (s76(6)). Once Ravi raises it, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt; if it succeeds, he is acquitted.

Loss of control. If the jury finds the force excessive, there is no partial defence of excessive self-defence, but Ravi may rely on loss of control (ss54-55 Coroners and Justice Act 2009). He must have lost self-control; terror can cause this, and it need not be sudden (s54(2)). The qualifying trigger is fear of serious violence from Sam against Ravi (s55(3)). There is no sign of considered revenge (s54(4)) or incitement (s55(6)). The final question is whether a man of Ravi's age with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint, in his circumstances (including the months of threats), might have reacted in the same or a similar way. This is plausible. If there is sufficient evidence, the prosecution must disprove the defence, and if it cannot, Ravi is guilty of voluntary manslaughter rather than murder.

Conclusion. Ravi caused Sam's death with the mens rea for murder. Self-defence, if not disproved, leads to acquittal; if the force was unreasonable, loss of control is likely to reduce the offence to manslaughter.

questions.q: Problem question. Kate works as a cashier at a supermarket. (a) Her employer mistakenly pays her double her usual monthly wage. She notices, says nothing and spends the extra money. (b) She takes her neighbour's lawnmower without asking, intending to return it at the end of the summer when, as she knows, its blades will be worn out. (c) She uses her manager's staff discount code at the till to give her friends a 30% discount, which they are not entitled to. (d) Angry with the manager, she sprays his car with washable paint, which costs £80 to have professionally removed. Discuss Kate's criminal liability.
markScheme: (a) Theft: appropriation by keeping/spending (s3(1)); property belonging to another via s5(4) and A-G's Ref (No 1 of 1983); intention to deprive; dishonesty (s2 then Ivey/Barton)
(b) Theft of lawnmower: appropriation; s6(1) borrowing equivalent to outright taking if goodness, virtue and practical value exhausted (Lloyd); dishonesty
(c) Fraud by abuse of position (s4) as employee expected to safeguard employer's financial interests; alternatively false representation via till (s2, s2(5)); gain/loss (s5); dishonesty
(d) Criminal damage s1(1) CDA 1971: damage includes temporary impairment requiring cost to remove (Hardman); property of another; intention
Correct statement of the Ivey test and rejection of Ghosh limb two
Considers s2(1) beliefs and lawful excuse under s5 CDA where relevant
Clear structure and reasoned conclusions on each part
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Overpaid wages. Kate may be guilty of theft (s1 Theft Act 1968). When her employer paid her by mistake, the extra money became hers in civil law, but s5(4) provides that where a person gets property by another's mistake and is under a legal obligation to restore it, the property is treated as belonging to the person entitled to restoration. In Attorney-General's Reference (No 1 of 1983) an overpaid police officer could therefore steal the excess. By keeping and spending the money she assumes the rights of an owner (s3(1)) and intends to deprive the employer permanently, since s5(4) treats an intention not to restore as such an intention. On dishonesty, none of the s2(1) beliefs seems to apply. Under Ivey, confirmed in Barton and Booth, the jury finds her actual knowledge (she knew she had been overpaid) and asks whether keeping it was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. It almost certainly was.

(b) The lawnmower. Taking the mower is an appropriation of property belonging to another. Kate plans to return it, so the question is whether she has an intention of permanently depriving under s6(1): borrowing counts if it is for a period and in circumstances equivalent to an outright taking. R v Lloyd held this covers borrowing until the thing's "goodness, virtue and practical value" is gone. If she intends to return it only when the blades are worn out and it is useless, she arguably falls within s6(1), although worn blades can be replaced, so a jury might find some value remains. Taking without asking is likely to be dishonest under Ivey. If the jury is not satisfied about s6, she would not be guilty of theft.

(c) The discount code. As a cashier Kate is in a position in which she is expected not to act against her employer's financial interests, so she may be guilty of fraud by abuse of position (s4 Fraud Act 2006). Using the code dishonestly abuses that position, and she intends to cause loss to her employer and a gain to her friends in money (s5). Alternatively, entering the code into the till system is a false representation that the customers are entitled to the discount, made to a device (s2(5)), so s2 is also available. Fraud is a conduct offence, so it is complete when she acts. Dishonesty is judged by the Ivey test.

(d) The paint. Under s1(1) Criminal Damage Act 1971, Kate damages property belonging to another. Damage includes temporary impairment that costs money to remedy: in Hardman v Chief Constable of Avon and Somerset, water-soluble paint was damage because the council paid to remove it. Here professional removal cost £80, so this is likely to be damage. She acts intentionally out of anger. She has no lawful excuse under s5, as she has no belief that the manager would consent and is not protecting property.

Conclusion. Kate is likely guilty of theft in (a), possibly theft in (b) depending on the s6 issue, fraud in (c) and criminal damage in (d).
